Triggers.value: People who are related to the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
I can't stop bad things from happening to me
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Daniel Lim was thirty-four when the robbery fractured his daily rhythm. It had begun as an ordinary evening walk in the downtown corridor, but the sudden rush of a man in a grease-stained work coat had turned the sidewalk into a trap. The attacker's weight pressed Daniel against the brick wall, and Daniel's own breath quickened to a ragged rhythm that ran parallel to the stranger's. What stayed with him were not narratives but sharp pictures: the glint of the man's signet ring, the frayed hem of his coat, the way the sodium streetlight caught the attacker's wide, unblinking eyes. When the man finally pulled away, slipping back into the evening crowd, Daniel was left clutching his satchel, the sharp, metallic tang of damp wool and old street iron hanging in his nostrils. He had come to believe that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he was-too open in his posture, too accustomed to offering rather than receiving. Some other chaplain, he thought, would have noticed the shifting weight in the stranger's shoulder and moved early. He was certain now that helplessness had settled into his daily rhythm; no matter how carefully he read a room, he could not stop bad things from arriving unannounced. Over the following months, those initial impressions hardened into steady habits. Daniel worked as a chaplain at St. Jude's Metropolitan Hospital, a role that had once offered him purpose but now demanded careful negotiation. The hospital's main corridor, with its rolling IV poles, chattering nurses, and steady stream of visitors, became a testing ground for his symptoms. Heavy breathing-whether from a postoperative patient in a nearby room or a visitor resting against a potted fern-caught him off guard, pulling those same visceral pictures back into focus. He learned to time his rounds to avoid the peak-hour rush, slipping through service elevators rather than the glass atrium. When the olfactory recall appeared, usually without warning, he would pause mid-sentence in the medication bay, inhaling sharply to locate the source. Was it the antiseptic wiping clean the counter, or the faint, familiar odor of damp wool and street iron that now lived in his memory? He did not argue with it; he simply adjusted. His avoidance accumulated quietly but measurably. He began leaving earlier for family dinners, declining invitations to the hospital staff lounge, and letting parishioners approach him through the chapel doors rather than chasing them down the hall. His widowed status, once a quiet companion, now felt like a quiet comparison; he watched couples navigate the crowded waiting rooms and felt a parallel steadiness in their shared presence that his own routine lacked. His symptom load, reflected in a PCL-5 score of seventy-seven, was not an abstract number but a lived tension that sat alongside his work, his memories, and his quiet routines. By the time Daniel sought clinical help, the weight of the event had settled into a steady hum. He sat in the consultation room, his hands folded loosely over his knees, and described the memories as they came: not as stories he told, but as frames he watched. He remembered the robber's heavy breath against his collarbone, the cold press of the man's knuckles, the sudden, sharp heat of rage that had flared in his chest when he realized the satchel was slipping from his grip. That rage did not fade with time; it simply waited for the right picture to surface. His character blame, his helplessness, and his self-comparison coexisted in his awareness without dictating his movements. What frightened him most was the recurrence-the way a crowded lobby or a familiar gait could pull him back to that same wall, same light, same breath. He hoped to understand why the world felt so heavy when he was supposed to be the one carrying it for others, and why he had finally stopped waiting for the street to make sense on its own.
